name: Indonesia
governanceModel: Non-binding ethics guidance and a national strategy roadmap, with a draft Presidential Regulation on AI ethics still in progress
debateTopics: Data localization and digital sovereignty vs. hyperscaler investment
Soft-law ethics guidance vs. a binding AI regulation
overview:
Indonesia's AI governance currently rests on non-binding instruments rather than a binding AI-specific law. The Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (Komdigi, formerly Kominfo) issued Circular Letter SE Menkominfo No. 9/2023 setting out nine voluntary ethical principles for AI — described by some trackers as the first such guidance in ASEAN — and has since been developing a National AI Roadmap (Peta Jalan KA Nasional) intended to operationalize the longer-run National AI Strategy (Stranas KA, 2020–2045). A draft Presidential Regulation (Perpres) on AI ethics, reportedly using a risk-tiered structure (unacceptable/high/low risk) with a two-year compliance window, was circulated for consultation with a version dated January 27, 2026, but available reporting does not confirm it has been signed into force as of mid-2026; Minister Meutya Hafid has publicly described AI regulation as a priority for President Prabowo Subianto's government in 2026, though exact timelines vary across secondary sources and should be treated with some caution.

Alongside this policy work, Indonesia has attracted large hyperscaler and chipmaker investment: Microsoft committed $1.7B toward Indonesian cloud and AI infrastructure (announced April 2024) and opened its first Indonesian hyperscale region, "Indonesia Central," in May 2025, while Nvidia, Cisco and telecom operator Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison launched a National AI Center of Excellence in Jakarta in July 2025 built around Indosat's Lintasarta AI Factory. How this infrastructure buildout interacts with Indonesia's existing data-localization rules under the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP No. 27/2022) remains an active point of discussion among industry and policymakers.

atAGlance.regulatoryApproach: Voluntary ethics circular (SE 9/2023) plus a national strategy roadmap; a risk-tiered draft Presidential Regulation on AI ethics has been under consultation but its enactment status is unconfirmed
atAGlance.latestMajorUpdate: National AI Center of Excellence launched in Jakarta with Komdigi, Indosat, Nvidia and Cisco (July 2025); draft Perpres on AI ethics circulated dated January 27, 2026
atAGlance.governmentInvolvement: Active on strategy and infrastructure partnerships (Komdigi-led roadmap, state-linked telecom partnerships with Nvidia/Cisco), but no binding AI-specific law is yet in force
atAGlance.industrialStrategy: Positioning as a Southeast Asian AI infrastructure hub via hyperscaler investment (Microsoft's Indonesia Central region) and the Nvidia/Cisco/Indosat AI Center of Excellence, alongside a workforce goal of training roughly one million people in AI by 2027
atAGlance.internationalPartnerships: Large-scale partnerships with Microsoft, Nvidia and Cisco on cloud and AI infrastructure; Indonesia also participates in ASEAN-level AI governance discussions
atAGlance.primaryPolicyFocus: Finalizing the National AI Roadmap and the draft Perpres on AI ethics appear to be near-term government priorities, based on ministerial statements, though official timelines have shifted

currentDirection.summary: Indonesia appears to be moving from voluntary ethics guidance toward a more formal, risk-tiered regulatory instrument, though the draft Presidential Regulation on AI ethics has not been confirmed as enacted and its timeline has reportedly slipped across 2025 into 2026. Government statements suggest continued priority on AI regulation for 2026, but observers should treat specific dates with caution given inconsistent secondary reporting.

recentDevelopments.text: Komdigi's National AI Roadmap white paper and the draft Presidential Regulation are reported to propose a 'Sovereign AI Fund' — to be managed by state investment agency Danantara under a public–private partnership scheme (variously reported for the 2027–2029 period) — to finance data centres, compute and AI-talent development, as Indonesia frames a longer-run sovereign-AI ambition. Details and timeline remain provisional.

Microsoft announces a $1.7B investment in Indonesian cloud and AI infrastructure — described as the largest in Microsoft's 29-year history in the country — alongside the elevAIte Indonesia program with Komdigi to train 1 million Indonesians in AI skills.

Microsoft opens "Indonesia Central," its first hyperscale cloud region in Indonesia; IDC projects a $15.2B economic contribution and over 106,000 jobs through 2028 (an industry-commissioned estimate, not independently verified).

National AI Center of Excellence launches in Jakarta, backed by Komdigi, Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, Nvidia and Cisco, built around Indosat's Lintasarta AI Factory — reportedly the first Southeast Asian deployment integrating Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems — with a stated goal of training 1 million people by 2027.

A draft Presidential Regulation (Perpres) on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, dated January 27, 2026, circulates with a risk-tiered structure (unacceptable/high/low risk) and a proposed two-year compliance window; its enactment status remains unconfirmed in available reporting.

Minister of Communication and Digital Affairs Meutya Hafid states that AI regulation is a priority for President Prabowo Subianto's government in 2026, citing AI's contribution to GDP; exact legislative timeline described inconsistently across secondary sources.

policyAndRegulation.title: Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP, Law No. 27/2022)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Indonesia's general data protection law, enacted in 2022 with a multi-year transition period; requires a lawful basis for processing, impact assessments for high-risk processing, and data protection officers — relevant to AI systems trained or operating on personal data. Some secondary compliance-guide sources cite an October 2026 full-enforcement deadline for the transition period, which was not independently confirmed against a primary source.

policyAndRegulation.title: Circular Letter on AI Ethics (SE Menkominfo No. 9/2023)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Non-binding guidance from the Ministry of Communication and Informatics setting out nine ethical principles for AI use (inclusivity, humanity, security, accessibility, transparency, accountability, personal data protection, sustainability, and intellectual property) for both public and private electronic system operators.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Strategy (Stranas KA, 2020–2045)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Long-run strategic roadmap identifying priority sectors for AI adoption — health, bureaucratic reform, education, food security, and mobility/smart cities — aligned with Indonesia's longer-term national development plan (RPJPN 2025–2045); not a binding legal instrument.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Roadmap (Peta Jalan KA Nasional, 2025–2029) / White Paper
policyAndRegulation.summary: An implementation-focused successor roadmap led by Komdigi intended to operationalize the Stranas KA strategy across pillars such as ethics/governance, talent, infrastructure and data, research, investment and priority use cases. A 'Buku Putih' (white paper) version was released for public consultation and is described as the foundation for follow-on implementing regulations and a proposed Presidential Regulation; it reportedly also proposes a Danantara-managed Sovereign AI Fund. No confirmed final adoption date was found in available reporting.

policyAndRegulation.title: Draft Presidential Regulation (Perpres) on Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
policyAndRegulation.summary: A risk-tiered draft regulation (unacceptable/high/low risk categories) with a proposed two-year compliance window, circulated for consultation with a version dated January 27, 2026; not confirmed as signed or in force as of this writing.

researchEcosystem.summary: Indonesian AI research is coordinated in part through the Indonesia AI Research Consortium (IARC), founded in October 2020 with members including Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM), Universitas Indonesia (UI), Institut Teknologi Bandung (ITB), Universitas Gunadarma, Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember (ITS) and Telkom University, later joined by Universitas Brawijaya in 2024. The National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) runs an AI and Cybersecurity Research Centre (established 2022) with applied projects in areas such as precision agriculture and remote-sensing law-enforcement tools, though available reporting names individual project researchers rather than a single clearly designated national AI research lead.

notableGaps.note: As of mid-2026, Indonesia has no confirmed binding AI-specific statute or regulation in force — the draft Perpres on AI ethics remains unconfirmed as signed, and existing AI guidance (SE 9/2023) is voluntary.
No frontier-scale foundation-model developer is headquartered in Indonesia; domestic AI companies (e.g. Kata.ai, Nodeflux) focus on applied/vertical AI rather than frontier model training.

Government and private facial-recognition deployments (e.g. Nodeflux's public-safety systems) have proceeded without a dedicated legal framework specific to biometric/facial-recognition technology, beyond the general Personal Data Protection Law.

debates.topic: Data localization and digital sovereignty vs. hyperscaler investment
debates.summary: Indonesia's push for digital sovereignty and data-localization rules sits in tension with its simultaneous courting of foreign hyperscaler investment from Microsoft, Google and AWS.
debates.expanded: Indonesia's data center industry has reportedly protested proposed data-localization reforms, arguing they could complicate the very foreign cloud investment (such as Microsoft's $1.7B commitment and its new Indonesia Central region) that the government has simultaneously sought to attract. This reflects a broader regional tension between sovereignty-driven policy goals and the practical reality that most large-scale AI infrastructure in Indonesia is currently built and operated by foreign hyperscalers.

debates.summary: Indonesian gig-economy platforms' use of algorithmic scheduling and earnings allocation has drawn scrutiny, including analysis suggesting a disproportionate burden on female drivers balancing caregiving responsibilities.
debates.expanded: Ride-hailing and delivery platforms operating in Indonesia rely on algorithmic systems to allocate jobs, set incentive structures and manage driver-partners who are typically classified outside standard employment protections. Commentary published in 2026 has argued that algorithmic scheduling can disadvantage female gig workers with caregiving constraints, and driver protests over algorithmic pay/allocation changes have occurred in prior years; the extent and consistency of these effects across platforms has not been independently quantified in available reporting.

debates.topic: Soft-law ethics guidance vs. a binding AI regulation
debates.summary: Indonesia's shift from a voluntary 2023 ethics circular toward a proposed risk-tiered Presidential Regulation reflects an ongoing debate about whether non-binding guidance is adequate as generative AI adoption scales.
debates.expanded: The 2023 circular letter carried no sanctions and relied on voluntary commitments from public and private electronic system operators. The subsequent move toward a risk-tiered draft Perpres suggests government recognition that binding rules may eventually be needed, but the draft's repeatedly shifting timeline (reported variously as expected in 2025, then early 2026) illustrates the practical difficulty of finalizing enforceable AI-specific regulation.
